link.title: SIMA: Scalable Instructable Multi-world Agent by Google DeepMind

entry.content:
(Report)

Training Environments

The Working: It’s Story Time!

Outcomes
Best Friend or Potential Enemy?
The Non-Violence Dilemma

Looking Through The Crystal Ball
Conclusion

Introduction

Alright, gaming enthusiasts! Get ready to step into the thrilling world of Google DeepMind’s latest creation — SIMA. Imagine a detective agency where the detectives are not just skilled at solving mysteries but are also ridiculously good at every video game. That’s SIMA in a nutshell, except it’s not your typical detective; it’s an AI that DeepMind has meticulously crafted in their lab of wonders.

SIMA, The Game Changer

Imagine a gaming detective who not only cracks the case but also knows exactly when to leap into action at your command. That is SIMA for you.

But what makes SIMA truly special is its ability to generalize across different game environments. Unlike previous AI agents that excel at a single game or genre, SIMA can apply its skills across a wide range of virtual worlds, much like a detective who can solve cases in any city they visit. And just like any good mystery, the title is a pun — no sleuthing required!

Behind The Scenes

Training Environments

Google DeepMind’s approach to training SIMA was comprehensive and diverse, designed to create a versatile AI agent capable of adapting to various gaming environments.

SIMA was trained on nine different commercial video games, specifically chosen for their open-world and sandbox nature, offering a wide range of elementary gaming skills for SIMA to learn. In addition to commercial games, SIMA was trained on four AI gaming environments. These environments provided more controlled settings to test SIMA’s object handling and perception of the physical world. The ProcTHOR paper is an interesting read if you want to learn more.

Training Methods

  1. Behavioral Cloning: SIMA learned by observing expert gamer-generated data, including gameplay videos, instructions, and annotations.
  2. Multi-task Learning: Training across multiple games simultaneously, helped SIMA develop generalizable skills.
  3. Natural Language Understanding (NLU): SIMA was trained to comprehend and follow natural language instructions within game contexts, enhancing its ability to interact with human players.

The Working: It’s Story Time!

SIMA’s brain operates like a high-tech detective agency solving the mysteries of the gaming world. Let’s break down this complex operation.

  1. SIMA has multimodal encoders dedicated to processing visual game scenes, audio cues, and textual instructions. This approach allows SIMA to gather a comprehensive set of clues from the gaming environment.
  2. Its cross-attention mechanisms take the diverse inputs from the multimodal encoders and fuse them together, creating rich, contextualized representations of the game state. This is like connecting the dots between different pieces of evidence to uncover the full story.
  3. An LLM component aids in understanding the nuances of instructions, game narratives, and the relationships between different game elements, allowing SIMA to “think” about the game world in a way that’s similar to human reasoning.
  4. Finally, the reinforcement learning module helps SIMA to learn from its actions in the game, understanding which strategies lead to success and which don’t. Over time, this module helps develop increasingly sophisticated and effective gaming strategies. Learning to Simulate could be related to SIMA’s ability to understand and interact with various gaming environments.

The Evaluation Process

Developers rigorously tested SIMA on 1,485 unique gaming tasks across nine skill categories. These categories included movement, simple navigation, resource gathering, and object manipulation, providing a comprehensive assessment of SIMA’s capabilities across various gaming scenarios.

Outcomes

The training resulted in several notable outcomes.

  1. SIMA demonstrated the ability to generalize, applying skills learned in one game to new, unseen games.
  2. AI agents trained on multiple games outperformed those trained on single games, highlighting the benefits of diverse training environments.
  3. In performance benchmarks, SIMA achieved a 34% success rate in some tasks, compared to a 60% success rate for human players (e.g., in No Man’s Sky).
  4. SIMA showed proficiency in basic navigation and object interaction, even when targets were not immediately visible.

However, while successful in many basic tasks, SIMA still requires further training for more complex interactions, indicating areas for future improvement and development.

Best Friend or Potential Enemy?

Google DeepMind has made concerted efforts to minimize the potential for violent behavior in SIMA by curating its training environments to exclude violent games and focusing on problem-solving and constructive interactions. However, this raises the question of whether such measures are sufficient.

The Non-Violence Dilemma

The extent to which AI can be trusted to act non-violently remains a contentious issue in the field of AI ethics. Proponents argue that carefully designed AI systems, trained on non-violent data and tasks, can be reliably programmed to avoid aggressive behaviors. They contend that ethical AI development practices, including rigorous testing and fail-safe mechanisms, can effectively mitigate risks of violent actions.

Conversely, skeptics point out that the complexity of advanced AI systems and their potential for emergent behaviors make it challenging to guarantee non-violent conduct consistently. They argue that even AI trained on peaceful tasks might unexpectedly develop or infer behaviors that could be considered harmful, especially when operating in dynamic, real-world environments.

This ongoing debate underscores the need for continuous research, robust governance frameworks, and interdisciplinary collaboration in AI development. For a critical perspective on trust and AI, see the paper In AI We Trust.

The NIST Framework

To address the broader challenges of AI development and deployment, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has developed the AI Risk Management Framework. This framework offers guidelines for organizations to better manage risks associated with AI systems, emphasizing trustworthiness and ethical considerations. Read more about this here!

Looking Through The Crystal Ball

Future versions of the system might be more adaptive in dynamic environments if it incorporates stronger self-supervised learning methods and improves its reinforcement learning tactics. This may help robotics applications, as SIMA’s capacity to comprehend natural language orders and navigate through intricate spatial settings may enhance human-robot interaction. Furthermore, the architecture of SIMA might be modified to enable more natural AI interactions for real-time decision-making in domains like autonomous systems and smart environments.

With more research, it’s possible that SIMA’s few-shot learning capabilities may improve, allowing it to quickly extend knowledge to new jobs with less data and opening the door for more effective and adaptable AI solutions.

Conclusion

As we look to the future, SIMA and technologies like it raise fascinating questions about the nature of intelligence, learning, and the potential for AI to not just assist humans, but to collaborate with us in increasingly sophisticated ways. Will future versions of SIMA be able to engage in creative problem-solving? Could they develop their own unique playing styles? The possibilities are as exciting as they are profound.

So, next time you’re stuck on a level, just remember — somewhere out there, Detective SIMA is probably solving the case while simultaneously learning three other games. It’s enough to make you want to rage-quit being human and become an AI!

entry.title: MISTRAL Mixtral-8x7B
entry.content:
(Paper, Code)

Contents

Introduction
The Creators of Mixtral
Open Source vs. Open Weight Models
The Model
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): It’s Story Time!
What Does An Expert Learn?
Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE)
What Are The Fun Nitty-Gritties?
How Good Is Mixtral-8x7B Really?
Conclusion

Introduction

December is an exciting month for everyone. With Christmas and the New Year knocking on the door, one is expectant of presents and new beginnings. But for machine learning enthusiasts, December is THE month; the best research from all over the world is presented in a span of one week at Neural Information Processing Systems, a conference more familiarly known as NeurIPS. Held between December 10th and 16th this year in New Orleans, with 3,584 published papers apart from a slew of tutorials and workshops, NeurIPS 2023 was a booming success. This GitHub repo presents an analysis of the conference data, making for an interesting insight into the bandwagon.

To comprehend such a massive amount of information is a difficult task, but fret not! You can leave all the reading to us — as we try to simplify these concepts to make it understandable for even dilettantes, we hope you enjoy our first ever post on MISTRAL Mixtral-8x7B, a technology that uses a very curious and ingenious neural network architecture.

The Creators of Mixtral

Before we dive into the model itself, let’s talk about its makers — MISTRAL AI, a French company founded in April 2023. Attaining a valuation of over $2 billion in December 2023, MISTRAL shows promising growth and great innovation. One of their tenets is the open nature of their models.

We are committed to driving the AI revolution by developing open-weight models that are on par with proprietary solutions. Source: https://mistral.ai/company/
We believe in open science, community and free software. Source: https://mistral.ai/

These claims give rise to a stimulating discussion. Are these models truly open source? This pressing question calls for a minor detour.

Open Source vs. Open Weight Models

Making a software open source entails releasing its source code for use, debugging, and modification. This includes use in proprietary software. Open source software is usually human readable, and is therefore, easy to comprehend and utilize. However, with regards to neural networks, the primary logic of the network lies in its weights. These weights are vector representations of everything the network has learnt. These, nevertheless, are not in human-readable format, due to which they are non-trivial for running, usage in other software, and debugging. Therefore, they do not fall perfectly into the open source category.

The question of how to limit the use of neural network weights while adhering to the Four Freedoms of free software is a subject of intense discussion, of which this article by GNU provides a detailed overview.

The Model

The Mixtral-8x7B model uses something called the Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) architecture. But to understand SMoE, let us first acquaint ourselves with the idea of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model as proposed in the Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts paper in the year 1991.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE): It’s Story Time!

Imagine a group of n friends planning a roadtrip. Each Friend excels in one area, such as driving, navigating, selecting a soundtrack, arranging an itinerary, and so on. One person, the Coordinator, decides which Friend’s skills are relevant for each situation encountered during the trip. In other words, the Coordinator decides which Friend’s opinion is most important during each step of the trip and assigns them the requisite role.

With each roadtrip, the Coordinator learns the strengths and weaknesses of each of the friends and modifies role delegation accordingly. Moreover, each Friend keeps improving on their own skill of doing their specific task.

In an MoE type of model, each Friend is a neural network called an “expert”, and the Coordinator is the “gatekeeper network”. Each expert network is very good at performing a specific use case, and the gatekeeper allocates a use case to one or some of the expert networks. Should the output be incorrect, the weight changes occur on a per-expert (or per-few-expert) case, where the respective expert(s) as well as the gatekeeper network learn the changes. That means that both of these are trained together for ensuring effective application over a variety of use cases.

Architecturally, with MoEs, each feed-forward network layer in the transformer model is swapped out with a MoE layer made up of a certain number of experts and a gate network. The input given to each expert is also given to the gatekeeper network, and while each expert gives one output, the gatekeeper network gives as many outputs as there are experts. The final output is given by the selector, which determines which experts’ outputs to consider. It can select the outputs of one or more experts.

What Does An Expert Learn?

The answer to this question lies in the ST-MoE paper. It was noticed that encoder experts had a focus on a subset of tokens or fundamental concepts. We could, for example, end with a punctuation expert, a proper noun expert, and so on. The decoder experts, however, are less specialized. The authors studied in a bilingual environment as well. While it would be ideal to think of every expert as having a particular language of expertise, the reality is that no expert has a particular language of expertise because of token routing and load balancing.

Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE)

Mixtral-8x7B is an SMoE model, but what’s that? Equipped with some background knowledge, let’s decode what this new term means.

Sparsity makes advantage of the conditional computation concept. Sparsity enables us to merely run a portion of the entire system, whereas in dense models, all parameters are employed for all inputs. In simpler terms, because only a portion of the network is active for particular inputs, sparsity in MoEs allows for scalability without increasing the amount of computation overall. Making lightweight models is another one of MISTRAL’s tenets, and this new architecture allows them to do exactly that.

The feedforward block selects from a set of eight different groups of parameters in this decoder-only model (hence the 8x). A router network selects two of these groups, or the “experts”, at each layer for each token in order to process it and contribute their output. This part is the same as the MoE model, with the only exception being in the number of experts selected at each layer.

Do read the Outrageously Large Neural Networks paper for an in-depth exploration of this concept.

What Are The Fun Nitty-Gritties?

Mixtral-8x7B is feature rich and easily accessible to the public. Here are some of its best characteristics:

  1. Open under the Apache 2.0 license
    It enables individuals to use, change, and distribute the software for any reason, with or without modifications. Users are also able to sublicense, but they must incorporate the original copyright and provide a license copy. It avoids concerns with patents and liability.
  2. Trained on data obtained from the open web
  3. 32,000 tokens for context
    The model is perfect for tasks needing a deep awareness of context because of its vast context-handling capability, which enables it to interpret and process bigger amounts of data. This is a crucial advancement, especially in cases where sophisticated understanding is required.
  4. Ability to be fine-tuned into an instruction-following model optimized through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
    SFT involves retraining a pre-trained model — typically from a large dataset — on a smaller dataset tailored to a specific goal. Gradient descent and backpropagation are used to modify the model’s weights in order to optimize for task-specific goals. For the purpose of improving performance, this procedure makes use of previous knowledge that was contained in the original model and tailors it to the specifics of the target task. More on this in this article.
    Models are directly optimized depending on user preferences using the DPO machine learning technique. Through pairwise comparisons, it learns how to enhance model parameters and formulates optimization targets as preference comparisons. The Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model paper talks about this in greater detail.
  5. Master of the English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish languages
  6. Strong performance when it comes to code generation

How Good Is Mixtral-8x7B Really?

Mixtral was contrasted with the base model of GPT-3.5 and the Llama 2 series. Mixtral performs on most benchmarks either on par with, or better than Llama 2 70B or GPT3.5.

Conforming to MISTRAL’s tenet of delivering high-performance and high-quality models, let’s take a look at the quality vs. inference budget tradeoff graphs on multiple factors for the Mixtral model family and LLaMA 2.

When it comes to biases and hallucinations, the base model of Mixtral performed really well w.r.t. BBQ and BOLD.

Mixtral has less bias on the BBQ benchmark than Llama 2. In general, Mixtral exhibits higher levels of positive sentiment on BOLD than Llama 2, with comparable variances observed within each dimension.

In short, Mixtral is a great model both in terms of performance and quality.

Conclusion

Mixtral employs such a simple concept to provide an elegant and efficient solution to typical language model problems, and we are all here for it! Free ways to access the model empower individuals to adapt and utilize it for their experimentation, while other industries are able to harness its excellent performance at a reasonable compute power. In all, we welcome this model with open arms and eagerly wait to witness more of MISTRAL’s innovations.
